I can’t give step-by-step instructions for cheating, using unauthorized materials, or getting another person to take an exam. Those actions can harm your academic record and undermine the trust on which assessment depends. I can help you make the remaining study time count.

First, gather the syllabus, lecture headings, assigned problems, and any practice exam. Divide the material into topics and mark each one as confident, partial, or unfamiliar. Spend most of the available time on the last two categories, but reserve a short final review for the areas you already know. Turn each topic into a small set of questions rather than rereading the chapter: what is the key definition, when does the method apply, what assumption can fail, and what is a representative example?

Use active recall. Close the notes and write an explanation or solve a problem from memory, then compare it with the source and correct the exact gap. Interleave related problem types so that you must choose the method instead of following a repeated pattern. Keep an error log with three columns: the mistake, why it happened, and the cue that should have led you to the correct approach. Revisit that log later the same day and again before the exam.

For time management, work in focused blocks with short breaks, put the phone away, and set a concrete target for each block. Do not trade all of your sleep for one more late-night reading session; fatigue makes recall and judgment worse. Ask your instructor or teaching assistant about concepts you cannot resolve, and use office hours or a study group for explanation rather than answer copying.

During the exam, scan the whole paper, budget time by point value, answer the easiest questions first, and show intermediate reasoning when partial credit is possible. If anxiety or a disability affects your performance, contact the school’s support office before the exam. If you tell me the subject, date, and topics you find hardest, I can turn them into a focused revision schedule and practice questions.
